• Other names: Bluefin nothos, African annual killifish, Annual Killifish, Blueband killifish, Rainbow killifish
  • Tank size: 10 gallons (~40 litres)
  • Keeping: easy; breeding: difficult
  • Dwellers: middle and bottom
  • Nitrate: less than 100
  • Diet: omnivore
  • Temperament: peaceful (with caution)
  • Life span: up to 1 year
  • Colour form: blue-orange

Nothobranchius rachovii is an annual species that has become a well-established model for aging studies. The genus Nothobranchius consists of about 100 species, typically 4–7.5 cm standard length, with striking sexual dichromatism: males are brightly coloured while females are mostly dull.

Nothobranchius rachovii is the most beautiful and vibrant representative of its genus. Beginners and aquarists unfamiliar with the species should be cautious and avoid impulse buys.

The species is fairly easy to care for. However, it has a very short life cycle, breeding is complex and time-consuming, and despite their small size, males are quite territorial.
This species is endemic to Mozambique. It inhabits the lower Zambezi and lower Pungwe River systems in Mozambique.

The natural habitats of Nothobranchius rachovii are seasonal pools and temporary water bodies where the water dries up annually.

Its life cycle is closely tied to the availability of water in these habitats produced by seasonal rains, and its rapid and short active life commences when rains fill the pool.

In the wild, the temperature is around 20–24°C, but it can rise up to 30°C during the dry season. These fish inhabit shallow waters where the current is absent or very slow-moving.

The recommended tank size is 10 gallons (40 litres) for 1 male and 2–3 females. For two breeding groups (2 males and 6 females), a 15-gallon (about 57 litres) aquarium is necessary as the males will establish and defend territories.

Nothobranchius rachovii are good jumpers. To prevent this: use a lid, lower the water level, keep floating plants and avoid stressing the fish.

Although these fish are resilient, their specific requirements must be met for optimal health and breeding. Ensure the tank is properly cycled before introducing them, and test water quality regularly with a kit.

Substrate: No special requirements, but a dark substrate makes the fish look more contrasting.

Plants and decorations: They need plenty of dark hiding spots using plants, rocks, stones, driftwood, coconuts, cork bark pieces, leaves, PVC pipes and other decorations. These provide shelter and reduce stress, especially if there are several males. Some aquarists place items such as coconuts in various locations so males can use them as shelters and establish a central point from which to control their territory.

Temperature: because high temperatures significantly shorten lifespan, keep them at 20–22°C.

pH: 5.5–7.0.

Hardness: GH 1–10, KH 1–8. The species can adapt to harder water, but this will also shorten its lifespan.

Water flow: stagnant water or very slow currents are recommended. Experiments showed that Nothobranchius rachovii ages faster under stress due to continuous water recirculation.

Filtration: it partly affects the water flow, so choose filters with minimal flow, such as sponge filtration.

Lighting: they do not like bright light and prefer subdued lighting. In planted tanks, lighting should be adapted to the needs of the plants.

Stomach content analysis showed that Nothobranchius rachovii is a generalist, mainly eating aquatic invertebrates (such as Cladocera, Copepoda, Ostracoda and Conchostraca) and mosquito larvae.

In aquariums they are not picky. They can be given a diverse range of frozen or live foods, including brine shrimp, Artemia nauplii, daphnia, fruit flies, moina, vinegar eels, mosquito larvae, cyclops, detritus worms, grindal worms, bloodworms, blackworms and tubifex worms. Large worms should be chopped into small pieces and flake food crumbled.

  • They are diurnal, so feed during the day.
  • The diet should be mostly protein-based.
  • They are prone to overeating (follow a 5-minute rule).
  • Feed twice per day, morning and evening.

They are plant safe and do not eat live plants. Planted tanks are highly recommended since they help reduce aggression.

Females are very peaceful and harmless. Males are brightly coloured and have a temperament to match. Besides aggression toward subordinate males, dominant males may also be aggressive toward females and toward other fish species, even slightly larger ones. With multiple males in the aquarium, each will claim and guard its territory.

It is better to keep them in nest groups, with two to three females per male. To reduce aggression, they can be raised and bred in groups of 5–6 males and 10–12 females without separating them. Isolating a male from the group, even for a week, can lead to problems. Keeping groups together from the start distributes aggression evenly and offers a larger genetic pool, but needs larger aquariums.

This diurnal species is lively and active, constantly on the move, especially at feeding time. It spends most of the time in the open, often checking the bottom and hovering in midwater, and is fond of dense vegetation and hiding places. It shows sleep-like states with short periods of inactivity, floating near the surface with no pectoral fin movement during the night.

  • Social: yes
  • Activity: high
  • Placement: middle and bottom
  • Peaceful: conditionally
  • Nippers: no
  • Jumpers: yes

Adult males are larger and much more colourful than the drab females.

Males show alternating light blue and orange-red stripes on the body and fins, an orange-red head, and an orange subterminal and black terminal band in the caudal fin. Colour, particularly on the head, may vary with aquarium conditions and water quality.

Females are olive grey-brown. The frontal scales on the flanks are iridescent light blue to silvery. All fins are colourless.

Scientists noticed that removing males from a population leads to larger females that produce fewer eggs.

Breeding is linked to the annual life cycle. In nature the water bodies dry up completely and all the fish die, so the fish lay eggs in mud for the next generation to survive drought until the rainy season. In aquariums this process must be replicated.

Maturity: 3 weeks to 2 months, depending on temperature.

Spawning: spawning is portioned and prolonged, with several small batches of eggs laid daily. During courtship the male tries to press the female to the bottom, adopting a vertical posture with head upward, making sudden movements, often lowering his lower lip and holding his head at about 45°.

Fecundity: females can lay 20–30 eggs per clutch per day, but the average is 4–10.

Eggs: adhesive, spherical, yellowish, demersal, with a large oil droplet that serves as a food source. Size about 0.97±0.03 mm. The egg envelope has two distinct layers that allow survival through dry periods.

Embryos: enter diapause for 6–9 months. Eggs will not survive if fully submerged in water for more than a few weeks. Eggs never develop all at once, a defence against false rains, so fry hatch in batches.

Fry: grow and mature extremely fast. In nature nearly 90% of embryos and fry reach adulthood. Average male length: 2.3 ± 0.15 cm at 1 month, 3.7 ± 0.22 cm at 4 months, 4.3 ± 0.35 cm at 7 months.

Breeding method:

  1. Put a male and a female in the breeding tank. Provide peat or coconut fibre as substrate, condition them with plenty of live food, raise the temperature to 25–26°C and lower the water level a bit.
  2. Instead of adding substrate directly, you can fill a small plastic jar with substrate (layer up to 2.5 cm). Some aquarists boil peat for 3–5 minutes before use, which cleans it while preserving its acidic reaction; boiling too long breaks down almost all acids, and the peat loses its ability to kill harmful bacteria that can destroy the eggs. The female deposits eggs in the substrate and the male fertilises them.
  3. After a few days of egg laying, return the breeders to the main tank, because females often eat eggs due to their fast metabolism.
  4. If a container was used, take it out of the water; otherwise completely dry out the aquarium to collect the substrate with eggs.
  5. Press the substrate slightly to remove excess water and let it dry until it easily crumbles in your hands while still slightly moist. Overdrying dehydrates the eggs and hinders development; insufficient drying can cause developmental delays.
  6. Place it in a plastic bag, sealed so that 3/4 is filled with air.
  7. Incubation usually lasts 6–9 months. Store the substrate at 21–25°C in a dark place, ventilate it once a month and check the eggs. If the peat is too dry, moisten it.
  8. Monitor the development of the embryos' eyes; once formed, it is time to add water.
  9. Put the substrate back into the water and keep it soft (4–8 GH) and acidic (pH 6.0–6.5).
  10. Once fry hatch, feed them infusoria and make sure they always have food.

Maintain water quality by regularly removing waste and leftovers. A few snails can be added as a clean-up crew.

Tankmates: ideally keep a species-only tank, given their relatively peaceful yet territorial nature. In community tanks, tankmates should be small fish that are not big enough to eat or harass them and that prefer or tolerate soft, slightly acidic water, such as neon tetras, Hemigrammus rhodostomus (brilliant rummynose tetra), least killifish, pencilfish, harlequin rasboras and pygmy corydoras.

Shrimp: possible to some degree. They are no threat to adult or juvenile shrimp, but newly hatched shrimp (about 2 mm) fit in their mouths and will be eaten from time to time. They are compatible with any freshwater snail.

Avoid: large and/or aggressive and/or boisterous fish, all types of crayfish and most freshwater crabs.

Etymology: the genus name Nothobranchius derives from the Greek "nothos" (false) and "branchia" (gill). The species name honours the German aquarist Arthur Rachow (1884–1960), who donated fish specimens to the Museum für Naturkunde. Described by Ahl, 1926.

Lifespan: in the wild, about 6–8 months on average; in aquariums around 1 year; maximum survival about 15 months. Aged fish show spine curvature, loss of body colour and deterioration of fins, especially the caudal fin. Survival of 4-month-old fish: 90 days at 20°C, 60 days at 25°C, 33 days at 30°C.

Description: adult size typically 2.5–4.5 cm; some reports of up to 8 cm. The body is long and laterally compressed. 15–17 soft dorsal fin rays and 15–18 soft anal fin rays; 26–28 scales.
